query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel, the onset of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments is governed by the integrity of its native iron oxide film. At room temperature, the naturally formed, compact oxide film limits corrosive attack; however, at elevated temperatures the film suffers thermal stress and increased cation diffusion, leading to spallation and localized breakdown. This loss of film integrity accelerates corrosion as fresh metal is exposed.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel with its typical ferrite–pearlite microstructure covered by a native, as-formed iron oxide layer
generation.intervention: A controlled removal versus preservation of the native oxide film followed by exposure in identical corrosive environments
generation.conditions: Samples will be tested under identical aggressive conditions (e.g., in 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution) at both room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (e.g., ~70°C). One set retains its native oxide layer while another set is cleaned to remove the oxide.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity, adhesion, and defect density of the native iron oxide film
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the intact oxide film acts as a barrier by limiting the diffusion of corrosive species to the underlying metal. At elevated temperatures, thermal expansion and enhanced ion mobility compromise the film’s integrity (via spallation or cracking), exposing fresh metal surfaces and triggering accelerated, localized anodic dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, samples with the intact native oxide film will exhibit lower corrosion rates compared to oxide-removed samples. At elevated temperatures, even samples initially possessing an intact oxide film will show significantly higher corrosion rates and a change in corrosion morphology (e.g., increased pitting) relative to the room-temperature condition and to the oxide-free samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its native oxide layer assessed at room temperature
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in aqueous environments where no additional protective scales are deposited, and within temperature ranges where thermal expansion significantly affects film integrity (up to around 70–80°C); behavior at extreme temperatures or in non-aqueous corrosive media may involve other dominating processes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold at which the protective oxide film loses integrity and the quantitative increase in corrosion rates require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of pre-exposure Q235 steel samples. For set A, retain the native oxide film; for set B, remove the oxide film using a consistent chemical etching procedure. Expose both sets in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature (~25°C) and a controlled elevated temperature (~70°C) for identical time durations. Monitor corrosion progression periodically.
measurements: Weight loss measurements to quantify corrosion rates
Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) to evaluate oxide film resistance and integrity
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) or optical microscopy to assess surface morphology and detect pitting or spallation
X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze surface oxide composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference is observed in corrosion rates and surface degradation between the oxide-intact and oxide-removed samples under identical conditions, or if elevated temperature does not lead to measurable deterioration or spallation of the native oxide film (as evidenced by EIS and surface analysis), then the hypothesis that the native oxide film integrity governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in Q235 steel would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
